item.title: Goldman Sachs: AI buildout to add up to 50bp to US core PCE, but the boost is temporary
item.description:
The analysis adds a structural layer to an inflation backdrop already strained by energy, which argues against easing and supports the case for central banks on tightening paths, including the Fed and the Bank of Japan, to keep a hawkish bias into 2027. Japan’s projected 0.3 point boost is notable ahead of this week’s BoJ meeting, where the key question is whether underlying inflation has reached 2%. For bonds, a temporary but well-timed price shock could keep front-end yields supported. For equities, the finding that AI lifts prices more than growth outside Asian supply hubs feeds into investor scrutiny of returns on AI spending. Oil remains the bigger swing factor, but AI now adds to the pressure from the goods side.

---

Speaking of inflation, coming today:

  • Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday’s BoJ decision

---

AI is showing up in inflation faster than in growth, and Goldman Sachs reckons the price bump will be temporary, though not before central banks have to sit through it.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says the AI infrastructure buildout will raise inflation in developed markets, with effects varying by region and fading through 2027
  • Memory prices currently add about 19bp to US core PCE; direct pressures elsewhere are around 0.1 point for now
  • Peak boost is put at 50bp for US core PCE and 20bp for US core CPI; non-US developed markets see an average 25bp lift to core inflation into early 2027, possibly up to 33bp
  • Japan is projected at around 0.3 point and the UK at about 0.2 point
  • GDP boost is modest at 0.3% on average across developed markets through 2026, with Australia highest at 0.6%
  • Goldman cites the concentration of data centre input production among Asian exporters as limiting wider spillovers

The global buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure is adding to inflation across developed economies, according to new analysis from Goldman Sachs, which sees the effect peaking at around 50 basis points on US core PCE inflation before fading through 2027. The bank stressed that the impact will vary by region and should prove temporary.

The main channel is direct price pressure from the hardware behind AI. Goldman estimates that memory prices alone are currently adding about 19 basis points to US core PCE, where those components carry a larger weight in the index. Outside the US, direct pressures are smaller for now, at around 0.1 percentage point in most economies, but the bank expects them to build as higher costs pass through to consumer electronics prices, which carry larger weights in non-US inflation baskets than in American measures.

On that basis, Goldman projects that price pressures directly linked to AI will lift year-on-year core inflation in non-US developed markets by about 19 basis points by the first quarter of 2027, compared with a peak boost of 50 basis points for US core PCE and 20 basis points for US core CPI. Taking all effects together, the bank estimates an average lift to core inflation of 25 basis points in non-US developed markets through early 2027, with potential increases of up to 33 basis points relative to long-run trends. Japan stands out at around 0.3 percentage point, with the UK at about 0.2 percentage point.

The indirect effect, through stronger economic activity, looks limited. Goldman estimates the AI buildout will lift GDP across developed markets by a modest 0.3% on average through the end of 2026, with Australia seeing the largest boost at 0.6%, the euro area 0.2% and the UK 0.1%. The bank attributes the small spillover to the concentration of data centre component production among Asian exporters, which keeps much of the economic benefit within a few supply hubs.

The analysis matters because it adds another source of upward price pressure for central banks already dealing with higher energy costs. Goldman’s view that the effect fades as memory price pressures ease suggests policymakers may treat it as a temporary shock, but its timing, peaking into early 2027, overlaps with a period when many are still judging whether inflation is sustainably back near target. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite
item.description:
The Shadow Board result adds to the case for a hike at the October review, although several members still favour a pause, so a hold would not be a shock. A hike paired with a clear signal of a prolonged pause could limit any boost to the New Zealand dollar, while a hold with hawkish guidance would keep year-end hike pricing alive. Oil is the swing factor: members tied much of the inflation risk to fuel prices and the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would strengthen the case for more tightening. The next inflation release is the near-term catalyst for NZ rate pricing.

---

Earlier:

  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation

---

Oil and a sliding kiwi have tipped most of NZIER’s Shadow Board toward another RBNZ hike, though the minority wants the central bank to let its earlier tightening do the work.

Summary:

  • A majority of the NZIER Monetary Policy Shadow Board recommends a 25bp OCR increase at the RBNZ’s October Monetary Policy Review, from 2.75% to 3%
  • Members cite renewed energy price pressure and a weaker New Zealand dollar as raising upside inflation risks
  • Several members prefer to hold and let earlier hikes work, pointing to a soft economy and weak labour market
  • Most expect the OCR to rise over the coming year, with year-ahead views ranging from 3% to 4%
  • Some say further tightening should depend on underlying inflation, inflation expectations and the pace of recovery
  • The next Shadow Board release is due on 7 December, ahead of the RBNZ’s Monetary Policy Statement

A majority of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research’s Monetary Policy Shadow Board has recommended that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise the Official Cash Rate by 25 basis points at its upcoming October Monetary Policy Review, which would take the rate to 3% from 2.75%. The group, which is independent of the central bank, said renewed pressure on global energy prices and a recent fall in the New Zealand dollar have increased the upside risks to inflation enough to justify another increase now.

The board was not unanimous. Several members argued that the RBNZ should give the increases already delivered more time to work through an economy that remains soft, with a cyclically weak labour market. One bank chief economist said there is a case to slow the pace of tightening, noting that while the short-term inflation picture looks more threatening, the medium-term outlook has not shifted, and that business and consumer surveys show no sign yet of second-round price effects.

Those favouring a hike pointed to a combination of pressures. Members cited the rebound in oil prices, a weaker currency, stronger-than-expected growth and core inflation that has stayed elevated, with one arguing that looking through these shocks has not returned inflation sustainably to the RBNZ’s 1% to 3% target band. Another member framed the decision as finely balanced, warning that with the conflict in Iran continuing, fuel-driven price pressures may prove less temporary than hoped.

A further view urged the bank to deliver the move and then signal a prolonged pause, arguing that clarity on the end of the tightening cycle would do more for business confidence than leaving the threat of further increases hanging over the economy.

Looking further out, most members agreed the OCR should rise over the coming year, with views of where it should sit in twelve months ranging between 3% and 4%. Some said the pace of further tightening should depend on how underlying inflation, inflation expectations and the recovery evolve. Several members flagged upcoming inflation data as important, and that release is likely to shape whether the RBNZ moves now or waits until year-end, as many commentators expect.

---

The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) is an independent economic research and consulting organisation based in Wellington, and its Monetary Policy Shadow Board is a panel of economists, academics and business leaders that meets ahead of each Reserve Bank of New Zealand decision. The key distinction is that the board says what the RBNZ should do, not what it will do. Each member assigns percentage weights to the policy options they prefer, and NZIER averages those preferences into a collective view. That makes the result a policy recommendation rather than a forecast or preview of the likely outcome. The two can differ: this month most members favour a hike, even though, as one member noted, many commentators expect the RBNZ to pause until year-end. NZIER says the exercise is also meant to encourage informed debate, show how a board structure might work, and explore how members could use probabilities to express uncertainty. The board is independent of the RBNZ, and members’ views are their own, not those of their employers.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citadel Securities warns AI trade has little margin for error as three risks converge
item.description:
The note gives a framework for the recent equity sell-off: a market priced for AI success has little cushion if returns slip, approvals drag or financing costs keep climbing. Heavy AI capex spenders with thin or negative free cash flow look most exposed, while diversified platforms with established cash flows are better placed. Oil is the wider macro threat, with Brent above $117 and reports of possible renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms keeping energy risk alive. That risk works against any easing from a Fed already facing sticky inflation. Credit is the channel to watch: widening spreads could raise financing costs for leveraged data centre projects even if Treasury yields fall.

---

Earlier:

  • The once Magnificent 7 are not so magnificent, but they still are large cap technology movers

---

Citadel Securities says the AI story has been carrying the market past a pile of other risks, and as faith in that story wavers, those risks become much harder to ignore.

Summary:

  • Citadel Securities says the recent equity sell-off shows investors want firmer evidence that AI spending will produce matching profits, with higher yields adding urgency
  • Meta’s Q3 capex of around $35bn exceeded operating cash flow of about $33bn, leaving free cash flow negative, with roughly $49bn to $59bn more implied for Q4
  • Ramp data show business AI token spending hit a new high in early October, but falling prices mean dollar spending understates usage growth
  • Political risk is rising: a Reuters/Ipsos poll shows 69% of Democrats and 43% of Republicans back limits on data centre construction
  • Pew data show 50% of US adults now see data centres as mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38% in January
  • Brent above $117, fiscal easing and tariffs are raising the cost of financing and running the economy, leaving the Fed in a difficult spot if AI investment slows

Citadel Securities has warned that the AI trade has very little room for error, arguing in a macro note that doubts over returns on the AI buildout are converging with political pushback and a costlier economic backdrop just as the stock market and wider economy have become heavily dependent on the theme.

The note reads the recent sharp equity sell-off as a sign that investors are becoming more demanding about whether extraordinary spending will deliver equally extraordinary profits, with higher bond yields making that question more urgent. Scrutiny now runs across the whole chain, from whether customers achieve real productivity gains, to whether model developers keep pricing power, to whether infrastructure revenues cover financing and depreciation costs. Capex has become a two-sided risk, the note argues: cuts would raise doubts about the investment cycle, while further increases raise questions about financing and eventual returns. Meta is cited as an example, with third-quarter capital spending of around $35 billion exceeding operating cash flow of about $33 billion, leaving free cash flow negative, and full-year guidance implying roughly $49 billion to $59 billion more in the fourth quarter.

Citadel Securities still sees strong demand for AI, pointing to Ramp data showing business token spending reached a new high in early October, though falling prices and efficiency gains mean dollar spending understates usage growth. Cheaper inference benefits customers, but supplier profits depend on how fast costs fall relative to prices. The note continues to favour diversified platforms with established cash flows.

Politics is the second pressure point. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 69% of Democratic voters and 43% of Republicans support limits on data centre construction, while Pew Research Center data show the share of US adults who see data centres as mostly bad for home energy costs rose to 50% in August from 38% in January. The note warns that permitting delays could add interest costs for leveraged projects and leave capacity arriving into a weaker pricing environment, and that AI-linked cyber concerns risk prompting broad restrictions.

The third layer is macro. Fiscal easing and tariffs have raised the cost of financing and operating the economy, while Brent crude trading above $117 a barrel this week adds to the energy squeeze. The note cautions that an AI-led investment slowdown alongside renewed energy disruption would leave the Federal Reserve facing weaker growth and an uncomfortable inflation backdrop, and that widening credit spreads could offset any fall in Treasury yields. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Carney says Canada has not budged as US trade deal looks less imminent than claimed
item.description:
The Canadian dollar had some deal optimism built in after the weekend remarks from Washington, so Carney’s comments and the Semafor report remove part of that support and leave USD/CAD sensitive to further trade headlines. A deal that eases retaliatory tariffs would still be a positive for Canadian exporters and cross-border supply chains, so any concrete breakthrough could still bring a sharp move. For oil, Canada is a major supplier of crude to the US, which keeps energy flows in focus whenever tariff talks shift. With the two governments framing progress so differently, traders are likely to want specifics before pricing a deal again.

---

Earlier:

  • US and Canada working on deal to ease tariffs on Canadian steel and auto imports

---

Washington says a deal is close, Ottawa says it hasn’t moved an inch, and the truth probably sits somewhere in the gap between the two.

Summary:

  • Canadian PM Mark Carney says Canada has not changed its position in trade talks with the US
  • Carney says any progress made is because the US has moved closer to Canada’s position
  • He acknowledged a slight intensification in the negotiations
  • Semafor, citing sources, reports a US-Canada deal is likely not as imminent as US officials indicated
  • On Sunday, NEC Director Kevin Hassett said negotiators were very close to a deal easing tit-for-tat tariffs, a view echoed by President Trump

Hopes for a quick US-Canada trade agreement faded on Monday after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa has not changed its position in talks with Washington, and that any progress made so far reflects the US moving closer to Canada’s stance. The comments came as Semafor, citing sources, reported that a deal is likely not as imminent as US officials had suggested over the weekend.

The pushback follows upbeat remarks on Sunday from Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, who said negotiators were very close to an agreement that would ease the tit-for-tat tariffs between the two countries. US President Donald Trump echoed that optimism.

Carney struck a more guarded tone. He acknowledged a slight intensification in the talks, but framed it on Canada’s terms, saying that to the extent progress has been made, it is because the US has come closer to Ottawa’s position. He also stressed that Canada’s own stance is unchanged, a signal that his government is not preparing to make fresh concessions to get a deal over the line.

Taken together, the two sides are describing the same negotiations very differently. Washington is projecting momentum, while Ottawa is emphasising that any movement has come from the US side. That gap matters because each government has domestic reasons to appear firm, and public claims of being close to a deal can be a negotiating tactic as much as a statement of fact. Semafor’s report adds weight to the view that the remaining differences are more than technical.

None of this rules out an agreement. More intensive talks suggest both sides see value in reaching one, and a deal that eases retaliatory tariffs would reduce costs for businesses on both sides of a deeply integrated border. The near-term question is whether the talks produce a concrete framework or a set of specific tariff reductions, rather than further statements of optimism. Until then, markets are likely to treat claims of an imminent deal with more caution than they did over the weekend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Solana trading bot Bloom drained of $947,000 in SOL as nine users’ wallets emptied
item.description:
The theft is too small to move SOL on its own, but it lands on a fragile tape. SOL has fallen about 14% in October, the weakest of the four largest cryptocurrencies, as spot Solana ETF outflows and a broad pullback from crypto risk weigh on sentiment. The more lasting effect may be on the Telegram trading bot segment, where users give up some control of signing in exchange for speed. If confidence in that model weakens, memecoin and short-term trading activity could ease, and much of that activity runs on Solana.

-- A Telegram bot lost nearly $1 million of its users’ SOL in 94 seconds. It says the keys were safe, but the blockchain’s evidence still needs explaining.

Summary:

  • Bloom, a Telegram trading bot, says about 9,408 SOL (around $947,000) was drained from 49 wallets belonging to nine users on 26 October
  • Bloom attributes the breach to a remote code execution flaw in a third-party module and says no private keys were compromised
  • Bitquery’s tracing found the drain across 48 wallets took 94 seconds and that every transfer was validly signed by the source wallet’s own key
  • Some drained wallets had been inactive for months, and the withdrawals appear to have been organised in advance
  • Bloom will reimburse affected users in full, has paused some services, and advises moving remaining funds to new wallets
  • The breach is limited to one application, not the Solana network, and is small next to April’s $285 million Drift Protocol exploit

Bloom, a Telegram-based trading bot that supports Solana and EVM networks, says an attacker drained about 9,408 SOL, worth roughly $947,000, from 49 wallets belonging to nine users on Monday, 26 October. The company has promised to reimburse every affected user in full and has paused some services while it investigates.

The theft is a breach of a single application, not an attack on the Solana network itself. Bloom says the attacker exploited a remote code execution vulnerability in a third-party module, meaning a flaw that allowed outside code to run inside part of the bot’s software. On-chain monitoring service Onchain Lens flagged the outflows to a single receiving address at 04:26 UTC, and early blockchain estimates put the loss slightly higher, at about $954,000.

The company’s account and the independent tracing do not yet line up. Bloom says no private keys were compromised and that unaffected wallets are safe. However, blockchain data firm Bitquery found that every transfer was validly signed by the source wallet’s own key, and that the full sequence across 48 wallets took just 94 seconds. Bitquery could not establish how the attacker obtained that signing authority. Some of the drained wallets had been inactive for months, and the order of the withdrawals suggests the targets were organised before the attack began. Until Bloom publishes a root cause, the claim that keys were not exposed should be read as the company’s position rather than a confirmed finding.

For users, the episode shows the trade-off behind the convenience. Bots that trade on a user’s behalf need some form of signing access, so a weakness anywhere in their software can put funds at risk, even when the underlying blockchain works as designed. Bloom itself has advised users to move remaining funds to new wallets with freshly generated keys.

The loss is small by Solana standards. In April, attackers took about $285 million from Drift Protocol, the network’s largest perpetual futures exchange, in what TRM Labs called the biggest DeFi hack of 2026.

The next thing to watch is Bloom’s root-cause report, and in particular whether it explains how validly signed transfers were possible without key exposure. Confirmation that reimbursements have reached all nine users would ease concern. Evidence of wider key exposure would turn a contained incident into a broader question about bot security. Any movement of funds from the receiving address is also worth monitoring, as a sign of whether recovery remains realistic.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

AI moved back into the spotlight Monday as Anthropic’s public IPO filing gave traders another reason to assess both the opportunity—and the enormous financing requirements—behind the industry’s expansion.

U.S. stocks moved higher, while oil pulled back. The dollar strengthened against all the major currencies in your closing snapshot, but gold still managed a modest gain. Treasury trading was more divided, with shorter yields rising and longer yields edging lower.

Anthropic: A big IPO—and a big test for AI

Anthropic filed for an IPO, applying to list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. The maker of Claude has taken another step toward becoming a publicly traded company, although the filing leaves the number of shares and offering price unset. Filing for an IPO is a step toward a listing; the shares have not begun trading. sec.gov

InvestingLive reported expectations that the offering could raise more than $100 billion at a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Those remain potential deal parameters, rather than a priced offering. investinglive.com

The growth is substantial. Anthropic reported more than $16 billion in first-half revenue, roughly 14 times the year-earlier amount. That gives investors evidence of rapidly expanding demand, but the company also disclosed substantial losses.

For traders, the question is straightforward: How much is that growth worth, and how much additional capital will be needed to support it? A successful offering would demonstrate continued appetite for AI exposure. It would also bring another major company competing for investor dollars. My takeaway is that enthusiasm for the technology and discipline about valuation will need to travel together.

Anthropic’s IPO filing put the AI growth story back in the spotlight. The breadth of Monday’s gains suggested buyers were looking across the infrastructure needed to support that growth. Data centers need chips, but they also need faster connections, storage, reliable electricity and cooling.

After last week’s pressure on technology shares, buyers made a stronger showing. The next question is whether earnings and spending guidance can give them a reason to keep going.

Lower oil offered some relief for inflation concerns. However, oil above $100 remains a meaningful cost pressure for businesses and consumers.

Gold holds higher; Bitcoin slips

The next test is follow-through. Traders have an improving equity tone and lower oil, but also a stronger dollar and substantial expectations surrounding AI. Earnings, the Fed and the market’s willingness to finance the next stage of the AI buildout remain the key themes.

item.title: Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday’s BoJ decision
item.description:
The services PPI is rarely a big mover for the yen on its own, but a reading at or above 3.7% would reinforce December hike pricing and lend modest support to the yen and short-dated JGB yields into Friday. A downside surprise would carry more weight than usual, coming after the sharp September slowdown in goods producer prices, and could lean against the yen by encouraging talk of a slower BoJ path. With an October hike effectively priced out, the yen’s bigger reaction is more likely to come from the tone of the BoJ’s outlook report and Ueda’s press conference than from this data.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
  • BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
  • Nikkei slips, bounces, as Iran oil fears weigh; ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027

---

Japan’s services inflation is running at a two-year high, and the BoJ’s real test this week is whether it is willing to say underlying inflation has finally reached 2%.

Summary:

  • Japan’s September services PPI (corporate services price index) is due at 23:50 GMT (19:50 US Eastern), with consensus at 3.7% y/y, unchanged from August
  • August’s 3.7% was the fastest pace in more than two years; excluding international transportation it was a softer 3.2%
  • The index tracks business-to-business service prices and is watched for evidence that wage growth is passing through to prices
  • September goods PPI slowed to 6.8% y/y from 7.6%, well below expectations
  • The BoJ meets October 29-30 and is widely expected to hold at 1.25% after September’s hike; more than 80% of economists in a Bloomberg survey see the next move in December
  • The key focus is whether the BoJ judges underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, something it has never declared since adopting the goal in 2013

Main article: Japan’s services producer price index for September is due at 23:50 GMT (19:50 US Eastern time), and while it rarely moves markets on its own, this release lands just days before a Bank of Japan meeting where the inflation narrative will matter more than the rate decision itself. Consensus looks for annual growth to hold at 3.7%, matching August’s reading, which was the fastest pace in more than two years.

The index, published by the Bank of Japan and also known as the corporate services price index, tracks what companies charge each other for services such as transport, communications, finance, real estate, advertising and equipment leasing. It is labour-intensive by nature, so it is watched as a gauge of whether rising wages are being passed through into prices. That makes it a useful cross-check on the BoJ’s view that pay growth is feeding a self-sustaining inflation cycle, rather than inflation being driven mainly by imported costs.

Context from the goods side has been less hot. Japan’s goods producer price index slowed to 6.8% year on year in September from 7.6% in August, well short of expectations, helped in part by government fuel subsidies. A steady services reading against that backdrop would suggest domestic price pressure is holding up even as some cost-push pressure from raw materials eases. One caveat: part of August’s strength came from international transportation, and excluding that component the index rose a more modest 3.2%, so the breakdown deserves as much attention as the headline.

The BoJ meets on October 29 and 30, with the decision due on Friday. The bank raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September on a 7-2 vote, and a hold is the overwhelming expectation this week. A Bloomberg survey found more than 80% of economists expect the next hike in December, with none forecasting a move in October. Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled there is no need for back-to-back increases, while making clear that rates will need to rise further toward a neutral level.

The bigger question for markets is whether the BoJ’s quarterly outlook report judges that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, a declaration it has never made since adopting the goal in 2013. A firm services print would add weight to that case and to December pricing, while a softer reading would give the board more room to stay patient.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US and Canada working on deal to ease tariffs on Canadian steel and auto imports
item.description:
False reports of 'a Canada-USA trade deal' aren't far off from the number of reports about 'peace in Hormuz' so I would take this one with a grain of salt. There has been some noise over the weekend about new trade negotiations led by Lutnick.

This report from Reuters cites two Canadian and four American sources that say the sides are talking about reduced tariffs on autos and steel. They're underway with broad discontent in US border states about tariffs and Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers now running against tariffs.

The report says a deal is possible before the November 3 midterms but that the US wants Canada to make further concessions

"If it happens, it'll happen fast. But my sense is that it'll be a narrowed deal, if it ever happens" a 'Canadian industry source' is cited as saying. The current schedule is for a rise to 50% tariffs on Canadian autos and steels from January 1 but Trump said at a rally on the weekend that a deal could come "soon".

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The once Magnificent 7 are not so magnificent, but they still are large cap technology movers
item.description:
The once-dominant Magnificent 7 are looking a little less magnificent. However, their substantial weightings in the broader indices mean they still command plenty of attention—and have considerable influence over the direction of the overall market.

Today’s trading highlights the increasingly mixed performance within the group. The major technology indices are moving higher:

  • Nasdaq Composite: Up near 0.90%.

  • Nasdaq 100: Up near 1.25%.

Nevertheless, three of the seven stocks are trading lower, with Meta down around 1.38%, Apple lower by roughly 1.40%, and Alphabet declining about 1%.

The group is no longer moving together. That makes the technical picture for each stock more important, especially with three major earnings announcements approaching:

  • Microsoft and Alphabet: Wednesday after the close.

  • Amazon: Thursday after the close.

In the video above, I take a look at each of the Magnificent 7 stocks purely from a technical perspective. What is the bias? Where are the nearby risk levels? What targets need to be broken to give buyers—or sellers—more control?

Microsoft: Between the moving averages ahead of earnings

Microsoft is trading just above its 200-hour moving average at $519.76, but below its 100-hour moving average at $532.42.

Trading between those moving averages leaves the shorter-term bias neutral. Buyers have support to lean against below, but they still have work to do above.

A sustained move above $532.42 would tilt the technical bias more in favor of the buyers. Conversely, a break below $519.76 would give sellers more control. Until one side breaks and stays broken, those moving averages provide the boundaries for traders ahead of Wednesday’s earnings.

Alphabet: Sellers have control, but an important support area is in play

Alphabet shares are trading lower by around 0.92% at $317.30, after reaching a low today of $316.60. Last week’s break below the 200-day moving average at $341.27 gave sellers more control, and the price has continued lower.

The next key support area comes between $311.42 and $314.90. That zone is an important short-term barometer for buyers and sellers. Hold above it, and buyers have an opportunity to stabilize the price ahead of Wednesday’s earnings. Break below it, and there is room to roam to the downside.

On a recovery, $324.25 is the first upside target, followed by the 200-day moving average at $341.27. The sellers remain in control. Buyers need to defend support and start reclaiming those overhead levels to shift the bias.

Amazon: Broken support becomes overhead resistance

Amazon fell below its 100-hour, 200-hour and 100-day moving averages last week. Those breaks shifted the technical advantage toward the sellers.

The stock is trading near $248.46, below the moving-average resistance zone extending from the 100-day moving average at $251.76 to the 100-hour moving average at $256.65.

For buyers, reclaiming that zone is needed to improve the technical picture. Until then, rallies remain vulnerable to sellers leaning against those overhead levels.

On the downside, the next support area comes between $244.42 and $246.45, followed by the 200-day moving average at $243.30. Those are the levels buyers will want to defend ahead of Thursday’s earnings.

Nvidia: Buyers try to reclaim the 100-day moving average

Nvidia is trading higher by around 2.67% at $216.57, taking the price back above its 100-day moving average at $214.41 after breaking below it last week.

That puts the moving average back in focus as a risk-defining level. Stay above, and the buyers have a platform for a further recovery. Fall back below, and today’s improvement loses some of its significance.

On the topside, last week’s high at $222.30 is the next important target. The falling 100-hour moving average is also near that level, creating an additional hurdle.

The buyers are making a play, but they need to hold the reclaimed support and then get through that overhead resistance.

Apple: A pullback within a stronger technical picture

Apple remains one of the stronger charts in the group, with the price still near its all-time high despite today’s decline of roughly 1.3%–1.4%.

A down day alone does not reverse a bullish technical bias. The more important question is whether the selling breaks meaningful support and gives sellers greater control.

For now, the broader technical picture continues to favor the buyers.

Tesla: A strong rebound approaches the next hurdle

Tesla is trading sharply higher, up around 6.14%, with the rally taking the price back above its 200-day moving average at $386.14.

That break is a positive development for the buyers. Staying above the moving average would help preserve the improvement.

However, the next hurdle is close. The 50% midpoint of the decline from the late-2025 high to the July 2026 low comes in near $398. Today’s high reached $397.27, just short of that retracement.

The buyers have made progress, but they need to get above—and stay above—$398 to strengthen their case. Otherwise, the rebound risks stalling at a logical resistance level.

With earnings approaching, the technical levels give traders a framework for judging the reaction. The announcements can provide the shove. Whether the price breaks and holds above resistance—or falls through support—will help determine who takes control next.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia offers cash to Houthis to stop attacks - report
item.description:
An extraordinary report from Israel Hayom says Saudi Arabia is seeking a ceasefire with the Houthis through a deal that would see $1 billion transferred to the Iranian-backed group via Tehran.

Citing unnamed Gulf diplomatic sources, the newspaper says Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman made a visit to Tehran to negotiate the agreement as part of today's four-way meeting with Turkey and Pakistan. One source went so far as to claim that the money was brought aboard the military transport aircraft carrying the Saudi delegation.

The report comes amid continuing Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and Iranian disruptions to tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, both of which have severely constrained regional oil exports.

Saudi Arabia confirmed the diplomatic visit but did not acknowledge any financial transfer. Riyadh has publicly maintained that it will not submit to military pressure or provide funding before the Houthis make territorial concessions.

The proposed payment reportedly relates to a previous agreement under which Saudi Arabia would fund public-sector salaries and reconstruction in Houthi-controlled Yemen in exchange for an end to attacks.

For oil markets, the possibility of a negotiated ceasefire is significant, particularly if it allows Saudi Arabia to restore disrupted production and exports. However, it would not necessarily resolve the separate threat to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The larger takeaway is that Saudi Arabia may be looking for a way out of the conflict even if it means making substantial concessions to Iran's allies.

The $1 billion payment allegation is based on anonymous sources and remains unconfirmed. Given the potential implications for oil prices, it warrants considerable caution.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The cost of intelligence is collapsing
item.description:
OpenAI is just out with a new model named GPT 6.1 Terra.

This isn't as strong as GPT-6 Astra but it's far more efficient and it gets to the heart of where AI is headed. AI is becoming a commodity faster than it is becoming an indispensable service.

Already we have the Sol model, which is near Astra at a fifth of the price but now we have Terra, which cuts the price in half again. OpenAI also touts the model as being particularly useful for automated computer use.

"Terra understands what’s on screen, takes action across apps, writes naturally, and is a more capable model for your whole workday with the efficiency to take on more of it."

I'm skeptical of the 'writes naturally' claims from any of the models but there has been steady improvements across all tasks. For markets, falling costs make adoption more attractive, but they also raise questions about the margins and returns on capital of the companies supplying AI infrastructure.

Ultimately, I strongly believe that all the benefits of AI will fall to incumbent asset-heavy companies that can use it to improve efficiency rather than model makers. Now the bulls will argue Jevon's Paradox and I think that can run for awhile (years) but models are getting so intelligent and cheap that soon they will have extremely cheap models that cover 99% of use cases.

Along that curve, the profits will shift from tech companies to productivity beneficiaries, with layoffs along the way. Think about a company with substantial labour expenses and relatively limited exposure to AI-related capital spending. If it can automate 10–20% of routine administrative work, the potential margin impact could be enormous.

As for users, here is a better look at the somewhat-confusing lineup of models that OpenAI is currently offering.

The Nasdaq was last up 1.0% and the big news today is that Anthropic has filed for an IPO.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold continues to find support between $3960 and $3996
item.description:
Gold sellers took more control last week after the price broke below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages on Monday. The buyers could not reclaim those moving averages, and by Wednesday, the price began to accelerate to the downside.

That sequence is important from a technical perspective. A break below the moving averages gives sellers the initial advantage. Staying below them—and then moving farther away from them—shows that buyers are struggling to take back control. Last week, the sellers got their break and followed through.

The decline extended below the early October low near $4064 on Thursday before finding a bottom near $3975. The price bounced into the end of the week, but the recovery left sellers with the stronger hand and buyers with more work to do.

The good news for buyers? The decline reached a swing area between $3975 and $3996, and that area attracted buying interest. Below that zone, the swing low from late June at $3942 remains another important downside target.

Those levels now help define the next move. If sellers want to extend the decline, they need to push below the swing area and stay below it. A break would then put the June low at $3942 in play. Getting below that level would open the door for further selling.

Today’s price action shows that buyers are still willing to defend support, although the trading has been choppy.

The early low reached $3978.18, within the $3975–$3996 swing area, before buyers pushed the price up to $4026.79. That rally subsequently reversed, sending gold back toward $3988. Buyers stepped in again, and the price has since recovered to around $4017.66.

So there is a battle taking place. Buyers have leaned against the swing area on two separate dips today. That gives them a level to define and limit risk against. However, holding support is only the first step. They still need to show they can break above resistance and sustain a recovery.

The first upside hurdle is today’s high at $4026.79. A move above that level—and the ability to stay above it—would strengthen the short-term recovery and give buyers a little more confidence.

Beyond that, the more important resistance comes near $4064.39–$4066. That area combines the broken early October low at $4064.39 with the falling 100-hour moving average near $4066.

When an old support level lines up with a moving average, it creates a clearer reference point for both buyers and sellers. Sellers can lean against the area to define risk. Buyers need to get above it to show that the recovery is gaining traction. Until that happens, a bounce can still be viewed as a correction within the broader move lower.

For now, sellers retain the technical advantage, but buyers are making a stand near support. Stay above $3975–$3996, and the buyers have a foundation to build on. Break below it, and the focus shifts toward $3942. On the topside, getting above $4026.79 would be encouraging, but reclaiming $4064.39–$4066 would be a more meaningful step toward taking back control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi, Pakistani, Iranian and Turkish security chiefs sit down in Tehran, agree to continue talks
item.description:
Iran hosted the first four-way meeting of Iran, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia in Tehran today, according to Fars.

The group released a short statement afterwards, noting that they had agreed to continuing talks. The lack of detail is naturally frustrating but this is undoubtedly a push to provide some kind of durable peace in the region.

Attendees:

  • Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman
  • Pakistan Field Marshal Asim Munir
  • Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin
  • Host: Mohsen Rezaei, identified as Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council

The four agreed to keep talking with a view to “strengthening cooperation,” including on regional peace and security. That’s the entire substance of the release.

WTI is down  $1.44 to $101.83 today as fears of US strikes on the weekend dissipated but the market still has no real clarity on what's coming next on the Iran file. The rumors about offers of peace and reopening Hormuz were doing the rounds today but nothing seems to have any real traction.

One line of thinking is that if Republicans lose badly in the midterms, Trump won't see it as a rebuke on Iran. Instead, he may lash out and escalate attacks, attempting to salvage his legacy by defeating Iran. The risk is that Iran remains a formidble force and launches a damaging attack on Persian Gulf infrastructure. Said differently, it could be a worse version of what we already have, with an even-more difficult path towards peace. In that case, the market will start to price in curbed oil flows for the remainder of Trump's term (at least). 

Also part of the equation is the Israeli election on Tuesday. Betting markets show a 30% chance of Bibi remaining as Prime Minister after the usual Israeli coalition-making, which can be a slow process.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The USD is stronger vs the CAD, AUD and NZD today. What do the charts tell traders?
item.description:
The USD is stronger across the major currencies today, including the CAD, AUD and NZD. The greenback is up around 0.24% versus both the Canadian and Australian dollars and approximately 0.35% versus the New Zealand dollar. All three currencies are trading nearer their session lows against the USD.

However, the dollar’s gains tell only part of the story. For traders, the next question is whether the technical breaks can be sustained. What levels keep the USD buyers in control, and what would signal that the momentum is fading?

In the video above, I take a look at each currency pair and outline the technical bias, the risks and the next targets.

USDCAD: Buyers make a move, but the 100-day MA remains a hurdle

The USDCAD moved above its 100-hour moving average at 1.40287 and extended through its 100-day moving average at 1.40442. However, the break above the longer-term moving average could not be sustained. The price is currently near 1.4037, between those two technical levels.

That leaves traders with clearly defined support below and resistance above.

Holding above the 100-hour moving average keeps the near-term advantage with the buyers. However, they still need to get back above—and stay above—the 100-day moving average to give the upside move more credibility.

A sustained break above 1.40442 would open the door toward:

  • 1.4082: The previously broken 38.2% retracement.

  • 1.4093: The 200-hour moving average.

Conversely, a move back below 1.40287 would weaken the bullish bias and put the 50% midpoint of the move up from the August low at 1.40149 back in play. Break below that level, and sellers would have more reason to push toward the 1.3950 area.

The buyers have made progress, but they still have work to do. The 100-hour moving average defines their risk. The 100-day moving average is the next hurdle.

AUDUSD: Buyers had their shot above the 100-day MA. They missed.

The AUDUSD moved above its 100-day moving average at 0.70317 on Friday and again today. On both occasions, the buyers failed to sustain the break.

That failure matters. A move above a longer-term moving average gives buyers an opportunity to take more control. When the price cannot stay above it, traders have to respect the rejection.

The selling has now taken the price back below its 100-hour moving average at 0.7016, shifting the near-term bias in favor of the sellers.

That moving average becomes the close risk-defining level:

  • Stay below 0.7016: Sellers retain the near-term advantage.

  • Move back above 0.7016: The downside break loses momentum, and the battle between the 100-hour and 100-day moving averages is back on.

On further selling, the next key downside target comes between 0.6989 and 0.6994, where the 200-hour moving average and a swing area provide a support zone.

The buyers had their shot above the 100-day moving average and missed. Now the sellers have their opportunity below the 100-hour moving average. Can they keep control and push toward the next support area?

NZDUSD: The 100-hour MA gives way. The 200-hour MA is the next test.

The NZDUSD briefly broke below its 100-hour moving average last Thursday, but that break failed. On Friday, buyers leaned against the moving average on two separate occasions and held support, keeping the recovery intact.

Today, that pattern changed.

The upside move stalled at 0.5707, just short of last Thursday’s high near 0.5709. Buyers could not extend the recovery, and sellers subsequently pushed the price below the rising 100-hour moving average at 0.56878.

That break shifted the near-term advantage toward the sellers. The price has since reached 0.5671, bringing the rising 200-hour moving average at 0.5663 into focus.

The distinction is important: breaking the 100-hour moving average weakens the recovery. Breaking the 200-hour moving average would give sellers another technical reason to press lower.

If buyers instead hold support at the 200-hour moving average, the pair would be caught between two clear boundaries:

  • Resistance: The 100-hour moving average near 0.5688.

  • Support: The 200-hour moving average near 0.5663.

Between those levels, buyers and sellers would battle for the next shove. A break below the lower moving average would increase the bearish bias. A recovery above the upper moving average would suggest the sellers could not build on their opportunity.

In the video above, I walk through those levels on each chart and explain what buyers and sellers need to do next. The USD has the momentum today. The technical levels will help determine whether that momentum can continue.

item.title: Broader US stock indices are higher after each held support targets on Friday
item.description:
U.S. stocks are moving higher today after a mixed performance last week that saw technology shares take the brunt of the selling.

The Dow industrial average managed a modest weekly gain, while the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite, and Nasdaq 100 finished lower. For the week:

  • Dow industrial average: +0.41%.

  • S&P 500: −0.47%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: −0.71%.

  • Nasdaq 100: −0.79%.

Today, the S&P 500 and both Nasdaq indices are bouncing back, with gains near 0.70%. That is an encouraging start for buyers. From a technical perspective, however, the next question is whether they can turn a bounce from support into a more sustained recovery.

Last week’s declines brought the indices toward identifiable support levels, and buyers responded. Now those buyers need to show that they can take back resistance above.

Holding support is the first step. Breaking resistance is the next.

S&P 500: Buyers defended support. Now the hourly moving averages come into focus.

The S&P 500 found buyers near the upper end of a swing area between 7,573 and 7,617, while also holding just above its rising 100-day moving average at 7,604.

That combination gave buyers a reason to lean against support. The swing area identifies a zone where price has reacted previously, while the 100-day moving average provides another reference within that same zone.

When multiple technical tools point toward the same area, traders have a clearer place to judge the strength of buyers and sellers. Holding that area keeps the recovery opportunity alive. A sustained break below would weaken that argument.

For now, support held. The next upside hurdles are:

  • 7,716.98: The 200-hour moving average.

  • 7,741.75: The 100-hour moving average.

Those moving averages are the next tests of whether buyers can gain greater control of the shorter-term trend.

A move above the 200-hour moving average would be a positive step. Getting above the 100-hour moving average as well—and staying above both—would strengthen the bullish bias further.

Conversely, if the recovery stalls against those levels, sellers would have a place to lean and attempt to push the price back toward support.

The S&P buyers defended an important area below. They now need to prove themselves above.

Nasdaq Composite: The broken 100-day moving average remains the key hurdle

The Nasdaq Composite’s technical position is more vulnerable after last week’s decline took the index below its 100-day moving average at 26,246.89.

The good news for buyers is that the selling stalled ahead of the September low at 25,831.74. Sellers had an opportunity to extend the decline toward that low but could not get there.

Today’s rebound has reached 26,164.45. That brings the index closer to its 100-day moving average, but buyers still have work to do.

The key levels are:

  • 26,246.89: The 100-day moving average and the next upside hurdle.

  • 26,164.45: Today’s high so far.

  • 25,831.74: The September low and key downside support.

  • 25,006: The 200-day moving average below.

A moving average that previously offered support can become resistance after the price breaks below it. That is why the reaction around 26,246.89 matters.

If buyers can reclaim that level and hold above it, the recovery gains credibility. If sellers defend it, the rebound could stall with the index still below an important daily trend indicator.

On the downside, a break below 25,831.74 would weaken the support structure and open the door toward the 200-day moving average at 25,006.

Nasdaq 100: The support floor held, but resistance remains overhead

The Nasdaq 100 found buyers during Friday’s trading near a support floor between 28,822 and 28,953.

Today, the index has rebounded to 29,213.76, putting some distance between the price and that floor. However, the recovery remains well below the broken 100-day moving average at 29,557.95.

That is the hurdle buyers need to clear to improve the technical picture.

Until then, sellers remain in play. They can point to the price trading below its 100-day moving average, even as buyers point to the successful defense of support.

The key levels are:

  • 29,557.95: The 100-day moving average and key upside resistance.

  • 29,213.76: Today’s high so far.

  • 28,822–28,953: The support floor, with 28,822.67 the specific downside break level to watch.

  • 28,108: The 38.2% retracement of the advance from the April low.

  • 27,854: The 200-day moving average.

A sustained break below 28,822.67 would put the 38.2% retracement at 28,108 into focus, followed by the 200-day moving average at 27,854.

The 38.2% retracement measures how much of the advance from the April low has been given back. It provides another reference for judging the depth of the correction and whether buyers can establish support.

Those lower targets remain conditional. Sellers first need to break the floor that held on Friday.

A bounce is underway. Can buyers take the next step?

The encouraging development is that buyers showed up near support across all three indices. That gives traders defined levels against which to judge the recovery.

But the upside tests remain:

  • S&P 500: Reclaim the 200-hour and 100-hour moving averages.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Get back above—and stay above—the 100-day moving average.

  • Nasdaq 100: Reclaim its 100-day moving average while continuing to hold the support floor below.

For now, buyers are making a play. The next test is whether they can push through resistance and force sellers to give up more control.

In the video above, I take a look at the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite, and Nasdaq 100, outlining where support held, the resistance levels buyers need to break, and the downside targets that come into play if the recovery fails.

item.title: US October Dallas Fed manufacturing index 13.4 vs 9.8 prior
item.description:
• Prior was +9.8
  • Employment 11.6 vs 15.1 prior
  • capex 11.9 vs 8.5 prior
  • New orders 9.3 vs 30.7 prior
  • Prices paid 55.3 vs 52.2 prior
  • Future index 38.1 vs 20.8 prior

The survey improved but that new orders reading is sending a conflicting signal from the future index. The comments in the report are often telling:

Beverage and tobacco product manufacturing
  • We continue to see pressure on profitability. We are profitable, but barely. The challenge is the increase in costs we are paying for our raw materials. The increase in diesel costs is the justification we are being told from our suppliers. Being able to give our employees year-end raises to keep up with inflation will be a further pressure on profitability.
Computer and electronic product manufacturing
  • Higher interest rates affect our industry in a big way.
  • A change in government in November will likely affect the future outlook.
Fabricated metal product manufacturing
  • Some product mix changes, but overall we’re forecasting a fairly positive picture over the next 6 months.
Food manufacturing
  • Geopolitics, labor issues and recession/inflation worries.
Machinery manufacturing
  • Business is strong, with many new existing projects ramping up, and we’re continually receiving new business opportunities.
  • Activity is up and down; right now we are up.
  • The data center bubble will burst soon, but a viable business model underlies it that will survive, just on a smaller scale. The creative destruction of the free-market system will prevail.
Nonmetallic mineral product manufacturing
  • It's difficult to find manual labor workers right now. We are hopeful the political climate will change in November and things overall will get better.
Primary metal manufacturing
  • We remain concerned about the ongoing USMCA negotiations, particularly as they relate to Mexico and the potential impact on the U.S. aluminum industry. Our industry appreciates that the U.S. Commerce Secretary recognizes the risks associated with reducing tariffs on Mexican aluminum imports. Such reductions could create opportunities for increased shipments and transshipments of aluminum products from Asia and other countries into the U.S. market, potentially undermining the intended protections for American manufacturers. China remains a significant competitive concern for the U.S. aluminum extrusion industry. Chinese aluminum producers benefit from government subsidies, and concerns regarding the use of forced labor in Chinese supply chains raise additional questions about fair competition. These practices can place U.S. manufacturers at a significant disadvantage when competing against artificially low-priced imports. We believe any changes to USMCA must carefully address these risks and prevent trade provisions from becoming a pathway for circumventing U.S. tariffs. Protecting American manufacturing requires trade policies that promote fair competition, enforce meaningful rules of origin and prevent unfairly traded products from gaining an unintended advantage in the U.S. market.
Printing and related support activities
  • Data centers spending money on flimsy steel and HVAC systems does not make the economy robust. Rates should come down for those of us that have to support the system in the long term.
  • We are getting to be really slow and low on work which concerns me greatly. Many of our competitors were slow this summer when we were busy with large projects we have done for many years in a row during the summer months. Now it's our turn I guess to be slow. 
Transportation equipment manufacturing
  • Fuel pricing and the cost of domestic product increasing are dramatically tempering a recovery in the freight market.
  • Outlook plans will depend on the midterm outcomes and the Fed’s interest rate action.

For background, the Dallas Fed’s Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey is a monthly gauge of factory activity in Texas, released on the last Monday of the month at 10:30 am ET. It’s usually the final regional Fed manufacturing survey of the month, following the Empire State, Philadelphia, Richmond and Kansas City reports, and it rounds out the regional read ahead of the national ISM manufacturing index.

The survey asks around 100 Texas manufacturers whether various measures of activity increased, decreased or held steady from the prior month. Each index is calculated as the percentage reporting an increase minus the percentage reporting a decrease, so zero is the dividing line between expansion and contraction. The headline most markets focus on is the general business activity index, which captures firms’ broad view of conditions. The Dallas Fed considers the production index its key measure of actual state manufacturing output.

The survey also tracks new orders, shipments, capacity utilization, employment, hours worked, raw materials prices, finished goods prices and wages. Each has a matching index for expectations six months ahead. The price indexes are watched as an early signal of cost pressures and how much manufacturers are passing them on.

The survey’s most distinctive feature is its anonymous respondent comments, which offer blunt firsthand views on demand, tariffs, labor costs, energy and policy uncertainty. Those comments are often quoted more widely than the indexes themselves.

Texas has a large, energy-heavy industrial base, so the survey is sensitive to oil prices and drilling activity. It rarely moves markets on its own, but it adds to the regional picture. The Dallas Fed publishes a companion Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey the following day.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: GBPUSD trades to new lows and tests targeted support
item.description:
The GBPUSD is trading to a new session low in early North American trading, with sellers pushing the price below the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the August high to the October low at 1.3342.

Earlier today, buyers leaned against that retracement level and managed a modest bounce to 1.3356. However, that recovery ran out of steam, and the subsequent break below 1.3342 has shifted the near-term focus toward the next downside hurdle: the rising 200-hour moving average at 1.33327.

With the price trading near 1.3334, that moving average is being tested. The battle between buyers and sellers is at an important level.

Sellers started with a ceiling above

The sellers gained confidence earlier in the Asian-Pacific session when the high stalled against the 100-day moving average at 1.33874.

That failure gave traders a technical reason to sell, with risk defined against the moving average. Buyers had their shot to push through a longer-term technical ceiling. They could not get the job done, and the price rotated lower.

Now, after breaking below the retracement at 1.3342, sellers are trying to build on that rejection by taking out an important hourly support level.

Why the 200-hour moving average matters

A move below the 200-hour moving average would be the first break beneath that indicator since October 15. That makes this more than just another price level on the chart.

The moving average has helped define the bullish side of the recent corrective move. Staying above it keeps some of that structure intact. Breaking below it—and staying below—would suggest that sellers are taking greater control.

The distinction is important. A brief move below a moving average does not automatically confirm a sustained break. Traders want to see whether the price can extend lower and whether a subsequent bounce finds sellers near the broken level.

If the price breaks below but quickly snaps back above, the sellers may have had their shot and missed.

However, a break with follow-through would open the door toward the next swing area between 1.3298 and 1.33103. On the way down, traders would encounter the upper edge at 1.33103 first, followed by 1.3298.

Buyers also have a reason to get involved

Despite today’s selling, the 200-hour moving average remains a potential support level for dip buyers.

Why buy when the price is moving lower? Because an identifiable technical level gives traders a place to define and limit risk.

A buyer leaning against the moving average is looking for support to hold and the price to rotate higher. If the price instead breaks below with momentum and remains below, the reason for that trade weakens. The level provides a reference for deciding when the idea is no longer working.

That does not guarantee a bounce or an exact exit price. It gives the trade a clear technical framework.

For buyers to show that they are doing more than temporarily slowing the decline, they would need to reclaim 1.3342. That would put the price back above the broken 38.2% retracement and suggest that the latest downside break is losing traction.

The next upside steps would be:

  • 1.3355–1.3356: The earlier corrective high.

  • 1.33807: The 100-hour moving average.

  • 1.33874: The 100-day moving average that capped the Asian-Pacific session high.

Each level reclaimed would improve the buyers’ position. Until then, a bounce remains a recovery within today’s move lower.

Sellers are making a play. Can they finish it?

For now, the rejection at the 100-day moving average and the break below 1.3342 give sellers the near-term advantage.

But they still need to get through the 200-hour moving average at 1.33327.

Get below and stay below, and the bearish case strengthens, with 1.33103 and 1.3298 the next downside targets. Hold support and move back above 1.3342, and sellers risk losing some of today’s momentum.

The sellers are making a play. The next test is whether they can turn that pressure into a sustained break.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers make a play below the range. Can they keep control?
item.description:
Last week, the bitcoin buyers had their shot.

On Tuesday, they pushed the price above the 100- and 200-hour moving averages—the blue and green lines—and that break gave them the technical go-ahead to probe higher. The buying subsequently took the price above the ceiling near $84,178 and to a weekly high of $84,774 on Wednesday.

That was the opportunity for the buyers to take more control. They had cleared the hourly moving averages and broken above a familiar resistance level. The next step was to hold those breaks and build on the upside momentum.

They could not do it.

The price rotated lower as risk-off sentiment weighed on bitcoin. On Thursday, the decline took the price back below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages, then near $82,225 and $82,400. The bullish technical picture from earlier in the week shifted back in favor of the sellers.

The failed rebound helped confirm the shift

On Friday, the price bounced back toward the 200-hour moving average, but sellers leaned against that level and pushed the price lower into the weekend.

That retest is an important part of the technical story.

A break below a moving average is an initial bearish development. When the price subsequently returns to that moving average and finds sellers, it provides additional evidence that traders are using the level to define resistance and risk.

For sellers, the trade becomes more clearly defined: stay below the moving average and the bearish bias remains intact. Move back above it and stay above, and that bearish view starts to lose support.

Friday’s rejection kept the sellers in control. The decline continued to a Saturday low of $79,146.

Today, another move lower reached $79,260, just above that weekend low. Buyers have therefore shown some willingness to defend the same general area, but the rebound has been limited. After bouncing to $80,400, the price has rotated back toward $79,779.

There is a difference between stopping the decline and taking back control. So far, the buyers have managed the first. They still have work to do on the second.

What keeps the sellers in control?

The immediate technical barometers are the falling hourly moving averages:

  • 100-hour moving average: $80,797

  • 200-hour moving average: $81,620

As long as the price remains below those levels, the short-term bias favors the sellers.

The 100-hour moving average is the first hurdle. Buyers need to get above it and stay above it to show that the recovery has some traction. A move above the 200-hour moving average would provide further evidence that control is shifting back toward the buyers.

Why emphasize “stay above”?

Because last week provided a reminder that a break alone is not enough. The buyers cleared resistance, but they could not sustain the move. Follow-through matters. A brief push above a level that quickly reverses can leave traders caught on the wrong side and fuel a move in the opposite direction.

Sellers still need the next shove lower

Although the hourly moving averages favor the downside, the sellers also have something to prove.

The weekend low at $79,146 is the next key downside hurdle. Today’s low at $79,260 stalled just above it, making that area the immediate battleground.

A break below $79,146, followed by an inability to recover back above it, would strengthen the bearish case and open the door toward the next major technical targets:

  • $76,052: The 38.2% retracement of the move higher from the June 30 low.

  • $75,597: The rising 100-day moving average.

Those levels bring the broader daily picture into focus.

The hourly moving averages help define the shorter-term trading bias. The retracement and 100-day moving average provide reference points for how far a larger correction could extend. They are potential destinations if selling builds, rather than guarantees that the price will get there.

The bigger question: A range break or another failed move?

Since September 18, bitcoin has spent most of its time trading between roughly $80,000 and $87,374.

Over the weekend and again today, the sellers have made a play below the lower boundary of that range. Now they need to show they can keep the price outside it.

A sustained range break should attract follow-through. If the price instead moves back above $80,000, that would be an initial warning that the downside break is losing momentum. However, the buyers would still need to reclaim the hourly moving averages to strengthen their case.

That leaves a straightforward technical roadmap.

Below the hourly moving averages, the sellers retain the short-term advantage. Below $79,146, they have a chance to extend that advantage toward the deeper daily targets.

Conversely, a sustained move above $80,797 and then $81,620 would put the buyers back in the game and raise the risk that the break below the range has failed.

Last week, the buyers had their shot and could not sustain the upside break. Now the sellers have theirs.

They need to keep the pressure on—or risk giving control back.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic files for IPO on Nasdaq, will use the symbol 'ANT'
item.description:
Anthropic has filed the IPO that was rumored to be coming today.

An interesting bit of trivia is the ‘ant’ mythology. South Korean retail investors were dubbed ‘ants’ back in the 1980s, a put-down they eventually wore as a badge of honour. The term has gone global since COVID, and especially this year as the Kospi went parabolic. Separately, the people at Anthropic have long called themselves ‘Ants,’ a nod to the company name and its all-in culture. Now they’ve chosen ANT as their ticker, no doubt hoping for the kind of gains we saw in South Korean markets earlier this year.

As for the IPO, it's going to be a complicated one with five classes of stock, with the 'A' shares to be public. The overall count includes 846 million shares of Class N stock pledged to a public benefit fund. Tha compares to 240.6 million shares for CEO Dario Amodei and slightly more for his sister Daniela, who is the President of the company.

In terms of the economics of the company and the industry, here are some notable snaps:

  • Do not expect to pay an dividends in the foreseeable future
  • Total debt was $6.2 bnillion as of June 30
  • Intend to direct meaningful portion of our resources towards ensuring that frontier AI is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed
  • For the year ended Sept 30, revenue from each of our top five customers reached a record high
  • Believe existing cash and cash equivalents sufficient to support working capital and other requirements for at least the next 12 months
  • About 250 customers with $10m or more in revenue on a TTM basis
  • For year ending Sept 30, trailing 12 months revenue rose about 1200%

There is no word on when shares will begin trading but expect it to happen in November and to be huge, with a valuation in the $1.4-1.8 trillion range.

Update: The company is going to raise more than $100 billion at a valuation of $1.5-$2.0 trillion. The target date is November 16.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why falling oil prices can trigger a stock market rebound before economic conditions improve
item.description:
Markets are forward-looking. Markets often rally before the economy has actually improved. While inflation may still be elevated and central banks may still be reluctant to cut interest rates, stocks can rally simply because traders begin to believe that the worst-case scenario is becoming less likely.

In the current context, oil prices are central to this because energy is one of the main channels through which the geopolitical shock is affecting inflation, economic growth and monetary policy.

Oil is an input cost for businesses, a major component of household expenditure and an important driver of short-term inflation. Therefore, a sustained increase in oil prices can affect the most important side of the central bank's mandate: price stability. 

If a geopolitical crisis threatens oil production or disrupts a major shipping route, traders begin to price in the possibility of reduced supply, pushing crude prices higher. Even before the disruption fully affects physical supply, the increase in energy prices can influence inflation expectations and financial markets.

The first effect is on inflation. Higher oil prices directly increase the cost of fuel and other energy products. They can also indirectly raise the cost of transporting goods, manufacturing products and providing services. If businesses pass these higher costs on to consumers, the initial energy shock can spread into broader inflation.

The second effect is on economic growth. Households have less money available for discretionary spending after paying more for fuel and energy, while businesses face higher operating costs and potentially lower profit margins. If the shock persists, consumption and investment can weaken.

This creates a difficult environment for central banks as they may face rising inflation and slowing economic growth, making it harder to justify monetary easing even as the economy comes under pressure.

The key point is that an oil shock can be simultaneously inflationary and damaging to growth. This is generally unfavourable for equity markets because it can put upward pressure on interest rates while weakening the earnings outlook.

When oil prices decline, some of this pressure can reverse. Traders reduce their inflation forecasts, lower their expectations for future policy rates and become more willing to pay higher valuations for equities.

The lesson is that traders focus on whether the decline also changes the expected path of inflation and monetary policy. If tomorrow the geopolitical crisis gets resolved, for example, traders would immediately start to reprice the negative growth expectations and buy equities. That's because traders would expect inflation to fall alongside oil prices and the central bank to adopt a less hawkish stance. 

Falling oil prices can trigger an equity rebound because they reduce the perceived risk of a damaging combination of persistent inflation, restrictive monetary policy and weaker economic growth. But the impact depends on the reason for falling oil prices. If it's just temporary, then the future outlook doesn't change much and the rebound would eventually fade. If it's durable, it changes drastically the previous expectations, making a rebound solid and long-lasting. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Brazilian markets headed for a rout after surprise Lula election win
item.description:
The peril of relying on prediction markets to invest in capital markets will be laid bare today as Brazilian markets are torn apart.

The EWZ Brazil ETF is down 25% premarket following the surprise win by incumbent President Lula over Flavio Bolsonaro. Betting markets had Bolsonaro over 75% after he led in the f irst round of voting earlier this month.

Polls showed a close race but a final push by Lula appears to have done enough as he won 51.79% to 48.21%, which translates into more than 4 million votes. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede so some of the weakness in markets might be about an uncertain outcome but it's mostly about a continuing left wing government in Brazil. The move also halts the march towards populism in latin America in a surprise turn for the region that could lead to some knock-on market effects in neighboring countries.

In the FX market USD/BRL is up to 5.60 from 4.97 on the eve of the election and that's a big part of the drop in the USD-priced ETF.

The drop in the Brazilian ETF today wipes out the entire year-to-date rally in the market.

Notably, Brazilian stock market have basically been dead money for years. The EWZ ETF is flat since 2014, though I'd note that it's now trading at around 8x earnings as the commodity-heavy index benefits from elevated global prices. With that, today's drop could be a buying opportunity (once the dust settles).

The market was clearly caught off guard by the results and getting squeezed. Note that back in May, the ETF was trading at $39 when Lula was favored to win; compare that to $30.89 in the pre-market with better global commodity prices now. 

Eamonn earlier highlighted how the market is pricing in an extreme scenario, via Goldman Sachs' playbook from Monday:

The bank said the dollar could rise as much as 10% against the real, long-term government bond yields could climb by about 200 basis points, credit spreads could widen by 30 to 40 basis points and Brazilian equities could fall around 15%. Goldman framed these as an extreme case rather than its central expectation, but the figures underline the scale of the repricing risk. 

In other words, the premarket is pricing Goldman’s tail case — and then some.

The next thing to watch is Lula’s cabinet. The fastest way to put a floor in here is a credible finance minister signal this week.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar higher as Fed, earnings and data flood loom
item.description:
The U.S. dollar is starting the new trading week higher, but the bigger story is what lies ahead. A Fed decision, a flood of corporate earnings and important U.S. economic releases will test expectations for interest rates, growth and the returns on massive artificial intelligence investments.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

U.S. stock futures are pointing modestly higher, while crude oil is down about 2% in the supplied morning snapshot. Diplomatic efforts involving Iran offer some encouragement, but the threat of renewed fighting and Tuesday’s Israeli election keep geopolitical risks firmly in the picture.

The dollar is higher across the board

The greenback has gained against every major currency in the morning snapshot. Its largest gains are against the Japanese yen and New Zealand dollar, while the euro and Canadian dollar have shown the smallest declines against the USD.
